The 2027 Aliner Classic LXE Packs a Bathroom Into "One of the Smallest Trailers" Out There
14 photos
Photo: Aliner
Compact and lightweight, highly garageable, easy to set up, yet packed with everything a pair of adventurers would need – surely that sounds like that fabled RV/travel trailer that is about as real as glitter-pooping unicorns. The Aliner Classic LXE is no unicorn, glitter or no glitter, but it does come close to being the perfect camper.
U.S.-based camper specialist Aliner has long dubbed itself "America's trusted camper brand since 1984," and for once, there are no factual objections to it. Aliner has been around for decades and their popularity seems to hold steady, if not actually boom as the years pass. The same goes for the feedback they get for their product, so they're definitely doing something right.
Their Aliner Classic LXE is a good example of what that thing is that they're doing so right.
Aliner could also take credit for making collapsible travel trailers mainstream, though they stop short of that. Their approach to the perfect short-vacation RV has always been the hybrid, collapsible travel trailer, which you can get either in standard configuration or with extra bells and whistles for more comfort.
Photo: Aliner The Classic LXE comes pre-loaded with those, so it's a complete solution in and of itself. Aliner packs HVAC , hot water, a nice galley, and even a wet bathroom inside "one of the smallest trailers on the market," so that explains its lasting appeal.
The LXE nameplate has been present in the Aliner catalog since the late '90s, but the Classic LXE iteration is more recent. It stands for "Luxury Edition/Executive," signaling that this is a Classic trailer with everything you need already included.
The Classic sub-series falls under the A-Frame lineup in the Aliner catalog, so that tells you that this is a collapsible trailer that pitches at camp in an A-frame shape. You also get an oversized dormer on the front and a smaller one on the back, and you have the option to make the front one a hard wall if you want a bit more sturdiness.
Photo: Aliner The Classic LXE travels compact , much like a boxy cargo trailer. At camp, in under 30 minutes, a single person will open the hinged panels on that box, pitching a camper that looks like an odd tent. Unlike a tent, though, this one has hard-sided fiberglass walls, actual sliding windows, a solid roof, an aluminum frame, and more importantly, it sits at least 14 inches off the ground.
Though Aliner says that this is a complete, self-contained RV solution, the Classic XLE is an upgrade to tent camping – but it's the nicest one around. It's something to get you off the ground, out of the cold or the heat, and under a dry roof, while you enjoy the basic creature comforts.
The Classic XLE rides on a single axle and coming in at 15 feet (4.5 meters) in total length and a width of 78 inches (198 cm). It's just 64 inches (162 cm) high when it's closed for transport, "growing" to as much as 121 inches (307 cm) at camp on the standard 14-inch aluminum wheels and 124 inches (315 cm) if you go for the optional offroad configuration with 15-inch wheels and offroad tires.
Photo: Aliner It's highly garageable and very easy to maneuver or tow, Aliner points out. At 1,930 lbs (875 kg) of dry weight, 180 lbs (82 kg) of hitch weight, and a gross weight of 3,000 lbs (1,361 kg), it's also compatible with a wide range of towing vehicles.
Aliner describes it as "true self-contained comfort without the bulk," and that becomes obvious once you step inside. This is a two-person camper, with a large queen bed available at the back when you drop the table and join the sofa to the side benches, a nice galley on the off-side, and a wet bathroom module on the campside.
If you're not unfamiliar to Aliners , you probably know how these "modules" look. It's a small block with a large counter, which lifts to reveal a shower and a cassette toilet. The counter becomes a hard wall, and you also get a shower to go around the shower.
Photo: Aliner It's obviously not the most elegant option around, but it is a bathroom inside a 15-footer.
The LXE also comes standard with an 18,000-BTU furnace, an AC unit with a heat pump mounted under one of the benches, a water heater that services the galley, the shower module, and the outside shower, and a kitchen that really lacks for nothing given its dimensions. It comes standard with a two-burner Euro-style flush-mounted gas cooktop under a glass cover, a sink under a separate cover, a microwave, and a 12V fridge.
Because of its highest selling point, the transformational capability , the Classic LXE doesn't offer storage in the upper part, which has to fold down for transport. Storage options throughout the camper will be limited, and that's probably also the camper's weakest point.
Photo: Aliner Standard features also include opening windows on all four walls, a multi-speed fan in the ceiling to keep the air moving, four stabilizer jacks, a bike rack receiver, and an 11-gallon (41.6-liter) tank for freshwater. Aliner also includes a gas connection on the outside, a railing for a table, an outside storage compartment, power outlets inside and out, and LED lights inside and out.
Options include two LP tanks with a hard cover, a hard wall for the front dormer, a solar panel on the same dormer, high wind lift assist that will add extra strength to the camper, and the lift kit with the bigger wheels and offroad tires.
Sale prices depend on equipment and options, but also on the dealer you get your unit from, averaging around $30,000 – give or take a couple thousand of dollars.

Guarulhos Airport © Leonid Andronov
By Alex Lennane
25 November 2026
Brazil’s busiest international air cargo hub is struggling to move freight after tighter export inspections filled its warehouse, leaving some trucks waiting days to unload and delaying the handover of imports that had already cleared customs.
Kuehne+Nagel said on Tuesday that some trucks which arrived at São Paulo’s Guarulhos Airport on Friday 20 November were still waiting to unload. Some airlines had been unable to collect freight from the terminal, leaving less room for new shipments.
The export disruption comes on top of recurring problems with import collection. In June, the airport warned that imports were arriving faster than cleared freight was being collected, tying up warehouse space and slowing receiving, storage and handover. It flagged the same imbalance again on 12 November.
Brazilian forwarder VL Cargo said on Monday that acceptance of new export freight had been temporarily suspended and advised customers to hold deliveries. The airport said that day its terminal remained open around the clock and asked hauliers to confirm a slot before sending trucks. It said perishables, live animals and special cargo were being handled as usual and gave no recovery date.
Lufthansa Cargo told customers it would rebook outstanding weekend shipments, Brazilian trade outlet FUP News reported. The carrier said the terminal had temporarily stopped handing general cargo over to airlines and halted acceptance of new freight into storage when the warehouse reached capacity.
Kuehne+Nagel said the disruption followed a Federal Police operation from 18 to 22 November and that police and customs officers were continuing inspections at cargo acceptance points and in airline storage areas. Brazil’s Federal Police announced an anti-trafficking operation at Guarulhos on 18 November. The airport attributed the backlog to intensified checks on dry export cargo, without identifying a specific operation.
Guarulhos accounted for 59% of Brazil’s air exports and 55% of its air imports in 2025, according to the airport operator. The cargo terminal reported a record 99,500 tonnes in the third quarter of 2026, up 14.4% year on year, excluding courier shipments. Automotive freight was the largest segment at 20%, followed by pharmaceuticals, chemicals and hospital supplies at 19%, and machinery at 12%.
Fruit and eggs accounted for 36% of Guarulhos’s air export tonnage in 2024, with papayas and mangoes making up nearly four-fifths of fruit shipments. Electrical and electronic goods and chemical industry products, including medicines, were the two largest import categories by weight, according to São Paulo state’s logistics plan.

1968 Chevrolet Chevelle 427 Is Rarer Than a COPO, Packs Dual-Quad Setup
11 photos
Photo: Geoff Stunkard's Zookeeper's Diary/YouTube
Introduced for the 1964 model year, the Chevelle was Chevrolet's first mid-size car. Aimed primarily at the Ford Fairlane , the Chevelle became part of the muscle car wars almost as soon as it hit dealerships.
The SS version came with a variety of high-performance engines, but Chevrolet also offered the limited-edition Z-16, powered by a 375-horsepower big-block V8. In 1970, the Chevelle gained the notorious 454-cubic-inch (7.4-liter) LS6. Rated at a whopping 450 horsepower, it turned the Chevelle into America's most potent production car.
However, some powerful Chevelles were also born in private shops. Although mostly known for Camaro-based muscle cars, Yenko also built a limited-series Chevelle using the COPO ordering system. These cars were fitted with 427-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) V8 engines at a time when mid-sized Chevrolets were available with mills larger than 400 cubic inches (6.6 liters).
The COPO Chevelle is even rarer than the COPO 427 Camaro . The latter was built in about 1,000 units, 198 of which were ordered by Don Yenko. The COPO Chevelle, on the other hand, was produced in just 99 examples. It's also far scarcer than the Z-16 and SS 454 LS6, but it's by no means the rarest high-performance Chevelle out there.
That prize goes to a lesser known 427-equipped model that was conceived by Dick Harrell. A notable drag racer, Mr. Harrell is also responsible for the COPO ZL1 Camaro, which he conceived for the Fred Gibb Chevrolet dealership. A year before that, however, he dropped 427-cubic-inch V8s in the 1968 Chevelle.
Much like Yenko, Dick used the L72, but he also built a few cars with the Corvette's L88 mill. Most of these cars came with 450 horsepower on tap with a four-barrel carburetor or 500 horsepower when fitted with a dual-quad setup. How many of these Chevelles were built? Well, Chevelle experts estimate that 12 units left the Dick Harrell Performance Center in Kansas City, but only five have been documented so far.
If you haven't seen one yet, a pristine example was recently on display at the 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals (MCACN) . And the story goes that it's the only Harrell-built street car out there. It's in perfect condition inside and out and has only 11,342 miles (18,253 km) on the odometer.
The Chevelle was filmed while being inspected by MCACN's Vintage Certification team. The program recognizes unrestored original classics by inspecting them for approximately three hours, including a detailed examination underneath the car on a lift. The certification team then provides each owner with a detailed listing of their findings in a comprehensive report.
There's no info on what this inspection unearthed, but given the low mileage, it's safe to say that this Chevelle is highly original and perhaps the finest surviving Harrell car. It's also likely worth well over a quarter million dollars. Hit the play button below to check it out.

MCACN 2026: Dodge Charger Sunroof Display Is Packed With Ultra-Rare Mopars
17 photos
Photo: Geoff Stunkard's Zookeeper's Diary/YouTube
The 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals (MCACN) was packed with rare and gorgeous muscle cars. We've already seen the Chrysler 300 "letter series" display , and now it's time to look at something even more special. The event showcases a collection of rare sunroof Mopars.
Chrysler introduced the sunroof as a factory option in 1969. It was originally available only on the Charger, but it found its way on other Mopars as well in the early 1970s. However, because it was rumored to leak, the sunroof was never a popular feature.
According to the Mopar Sunroof Registry, only about 13,000 units were produced through 1974. The figure includes vehicles built by the Dodge, Plymouth, and Chrysler divisions. About two thirds of these cars were sold in 1973 and 1974.
The MCACN display included 13 sunroof Mopars , all of the Dodge Charger variety. Examples from all but the 1972 model year were present, and some are incredibly rare.
Photo: Corner Classic Car Hunter/YouTube The oldest example is a 1969 Charger R/T SE. Dodge sold only 391 units that year, and only 131 were equipped as R/T models. It's unclear how many were SE versions, but this Charger is basically a one-of-one rig thanks to its options list.
Owned by Tim Wellborn, this R/T SE was produced as a dealer demo car and was fitted with all the available options except for the passenger-side mirror. It also sports an unusual color combo. It's a yellow car with a white stripe, plus a green interior and green vinyl top.
The 1970 model year section includes three examples. Production included only 175 units. Two of these cars are R/T models, of which 112 were made. One has a Hemi under the hood, which makes it one of only two equipped with the sunroof.
The second R/T is an SE with a 440 Six-Pack unit. It's part of a batch of 15 identical demo cars built during the second day of production. All were loaded with options and painted Hemi Orange.
Photo: Corner Classic Car Hunter/YouTube The third 1970 Charger is a 500, of which only 54 were equipped with sunroofs. However, this one is also an SE, so that number is much smaller. This Mopar is a fully-fledged survivor with just 28,000 miles (45,062 km) on the odometer.
The 1971 model year had the best representation, with no fewer than five units on display. Tim Wellborn brought two vehicles to the show, including an R/T in triple-black . It's one of 30 units fitted with the R/T package, out of a total of 210 Chargers equipped with the sunroof that year.
His second sunroof Charger is an SE that's also loaded with options. This car was built for a company representative and got all the available goodies save for the headlamp washers. It cost in excess of $5,000 at the time. Originally F7 green, the car was repainted F8 green by Wellborn.
Two more SE-spec 1971 Chargers were hauled to the show; one finished in light blue, and another in black with a white vinyl top. The fifth example is actually a Super Bee, which was based on the Charger platform in 1971. Only nine Super Bees were ordered with the sunroof.
Photo: Geoff Stunkard's Zookeeper's Diary/YouTube None of the 488 sunroof Chargers built in 1972 were at the show, but the display included a pair of 1973 versions . The option had become a bit more popular at the time, with 3,097 units sold. Both are non-SE models, of which only 603 examples were made.
Finally, we have a pair of 1974-model-year Chargers on display. Dodge sold 2,388 sunroof models that year, but it's unclear how many were regular coupes and hardtops or SE versions.
You can check them all out in the videos below. The first one shows Tim Wellborn taking about his private trio, while the second video documents all 13 examples.

Detroit's Automakers Are Being Asked to Build America's Drone Supply Chain
29 photos
Photo: General Motors
General Motors could soon be making propulsion systems for military drones. The proposed motors would be closer in size to something found in a riding lawn mower than a small block or the Mongoose turbo diesel, making said motors a very different proposition for Detroit's largest automaker.
Pentagon officials, as reported by the Wall Street Journal, are in preliminary discussions with General Motors, the Ford Motor Company, the folks at Magna International, and companies outside the automotive industry. Said talks are centered on supplying vital components, including motors, lidar sensors, actuators, and so forth. Drone companies would remain fully responsible for the production of the aircraft themselves.
No agreement has been finalized thus far, with GM declining to comment on the specific proposal. Magna, on the other hand, confirmed preliminary discussions. Ford's involvement may be a little different. Although the Wall Street Journal included the Blue Oval among the companies approached by the Pentagon, it has been revealed that Ford is currently focused on military vehicles and its recent investment in Revolution Space .
In other words, ruggedized trucks for the military and the satellite business. Turning our attention back to General Motors, there is a precedent that has to be highlighted. GM's defense division has been working with Lockheed Martin to make housing components for the PAC-3 interceptor missile used by Patriot systems, with PAC-3 being a very expensive surface-to-air design.
Lockheed Martin announced in September 2026 that the first components had been delivered less than a month after the contract was signed, with General Motors bringing its commercial manufacturing capabilities to the defense program. Building production capacity quickly is the name of the game here.
Photo: Ford UK / General Dynamics UK Presumably, the Pentagon wants to replicate that performance with its next military drones. General Motors has literal decades of experience with casting, machining, electric propulsion systems, and very complex supply chains. On its own, General Motors can easily coordinate suppliers, purchase industrial quantities of materials, and run production processes at scale.
Most young drone manufacturers cannot match that, and US-based drone manufacturers are a bit lacking in this regard. The General Atomics MQ-1 Predator pioneered modern unmanned aerial missions in the 1990s, and the MQ-9 Reaper is now the best-known frontline armed drone in US military service. Fewer than 600 units of the MQ-9 Reaper have been produced to date, partly due to its exorbitant price. A combat-configured drone costs more than $30 million.
Making a missile housing is a different thing from supplying drone components, though, especially powertrain components. GM could be facing rapidly evolving propulsion designs, changing military requirements, and fierce pressure to keep unit costs low. The Pentagon hasn't made the procurement side of the biz attractive to outside manufacturers either.
Per the WSJ, six separate efforts were once underway to develop a one-way attack drone. All were pursuing the same goal, yet working to different specifications. That kind of duplication is the stuff of nightmares for suppliers, and looking at the bigger picture, an automaker cannot efficiently invest in a production line when the Pentagon has yet to decide which version of the subject component it wants.
The Pentagon estimates the military drone market could reach $20 to $30 billion per annum, all while its Drone Dominance Program has no more than $1.1 billion to produce more than 200,000 one-way attach drones by 2027. The $1.1 billion initiative also covers lethal payloads and modular warheads.

Changes to U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect October 30, adding 100 product classifications to the list subject to a 50% additional tariff and removing 22. Newly covered products include certain valves, carpets, waste products and cocoa powder. Products removed from the list include certain plywood sheets, paper products, machinery, refrigeration equipment and packaging materials.
What’s Related
The October 23 presidential proclamation revised which products face the additional tariff under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. The changes apply to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from a warehouse for consumption on or after October 30. The additional tariff applies on top of any applicable Section 232 duties.
On November 14, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the countries were making progress in trade talks, though no agreement had been reached. He said protecting Canada’s automotive industry remained a priority. With talks still underway, importers need to know which products are affected now, whether their customs filings reflect the changes, and what the revised duties mean for their costs.
Start with product classification
A product’s code in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) helps determine what duties an importer owes. A change in tariff coverage can raise or lower the cost of importing a product even when its classification stays the same.
Importers should match the revised list against the codes they use for goods sourced from Canada. Products with broad descriptions or incomplete specifications deserve a closer look. A precise description of what a product is made of and how it’s used can help teams confirm the right code. When a classification is uncertain, current customs guidance and rulings can help resolve the question.
Check origin and customs records
A product shipped from Canada may have a different country of origin for customs purposes. That distinction matters when components move between the United States, Canada, and Mexico during manufacturing . Importers should keep supplier records and manufacturing details that show how they determined the product’s origin.
Each tariff measure has its own rules for how it interacts with trade agreements. The additional Section 338 tariff applies to covered products even when they qualify for preferential treatment under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).
Commercial invoices, packing lists, bills of lading, and origin records should match the information used in customs declarations. A vague invoice description or an outdated classification in a product record can make it harder to confirm what duty applies. For companies with thousands of items and multiple suppliers, keeping product details in one place makes it easier to find affected items and give customs brokers the information they need.
Work out what the changes will cost
Once importers identify affected products, they can recalculate landed costs. That means accounting for applicable duties and other charges, as well as any quotas, exclusions, or exemptions that affect the total. The results can inform purchasing decisions, inventory plans, and customer pricing.
An importer whose refrigeration equipment falls under one of the removed codes may pay less to bring that equipment into the United States. An importer whose valves fall under one of the newly covered codes may face a substantial increase. The financial impact depends on each item's classification and which duties apply.
Connecting tariff changes to product records, purchase orders, and shipments gives leaders a clearer picture of how much they may owe and when. That timing matters if a company needs to adjust prices, review a supplier agreement, or make a purchasing decision before its next shipment arrives.
Make tariff monitoring part of the routine
The October 23 proclamation gave importers one week before the changes took effect. U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued filing guidance identifying affected classifications and explaining how to handle entries. A company that reviews tariffs only during scheduled compliance audits could miss changes that affect shipments already in transit.
Importers need a process to check government announcements, match affected tariff codes to their products and update duty calculations and filing instructions. Automated tools can flag products for review across a large catalog. Customs specialists still need to look at cases where a product’s classification or origin is unclear, or where the new rules leave room for interpretation.
Teams also need a way to get changes to the people who act on them. A customs broker may need revised filing instructions for an upcoming entry, while a buyer may need an updated cost before placing the next order. Both decisions depend on having current information about the product and the shipment.
Plan around today’s rules
Companies should keep watching for announcements from both governments as trade talks continue. Until a change formally takes effect, importers need to plan around the rules that apply to their shipments today. With current product records and a regular review process, they can see sooner which goods are affected, how much costs could change, and where an entry needs a closer look.
Shannon Hynds is CEO of Quickcode.

By Alex Lennane
25 November 2026
Some airlines are agreeing alternative liability terms with larger freight forwarders under IATA’s revised direct air waybill (DAWB) framework, but smaller firms have little leverage to secure similar arrangements, the Airforwarders Association (AfA) has warned.
“If an airline says no, the forwarder either accepts the default terms or moves the cargo to another carrier,” AfA chief executive Steve Smith told The Loadstar .
“A global standard shouldn’t only work for companies big enough to negotiate their way out of it.”
Under the framework, effective since 1 July, a forwarder tendering cargo as agent for a shipper named on the airline’s air waybill assumes the shipper obligations that would apply if it were shipping in its own name, unless it agrees alternative bilateral terms with the carrier.
Mr Smith said some airlines were agreeing terms with larger forwarding customers. But negotiating separately with a dozen carriers, often through general sales agents, was not a realistic solution for a small or midsized forwarder with limited bargaining power.
“Since July, members have told us they can’t be sure which terms apply from one airline to the next,” he said. “Some have been asked to accept the new default without a separate agreement in place.”
He added: “Airlines don’t benefit from a patchwork either, because it adds paperwork on their side too.”
IATA declined to answer The Loadstar’s questions about the associations’ legal objections, whether it would consider revising the framework, or the status of the review requested by FIATA. It also declined to say whether it knew of claims under the revised provisions or alternative bilateral agreements.
Its refusal leaves those questions unanswered as forwarder associations seek changes to rules already in force across its member airlines.
In September, however, IATA told The Loadstar the provisions applied across member airlines and that carriers and forwarders could agree different terms.
It said the changes addressed a safety-related liability gap that left airlines exposed to improperly prepared cargo where they had little or no relationship with the underlying shipper.
Mr Smith said there was no reliable industry figure for DAWB usage. They accounted for a minority of volume for most forwarders, but were used where the underlying shipper needed to appear on the airline’s own document.
Examples included letters of credit and other trade-finance paperwork, certain export-control and customs requirements, and shipments booked through a forwarder using the shipper’s own airline rates.
“Even a small share matters, because the exposure applies to every shipment, and smaller forwarders are least able to absorb a single large claim,” he said.
AfA was unaware of any claims, insurance exclusions or premium increases linked to the revised provisions. But Mr Smith said the association wanted to address the exposure before a serious incident.
“We would rather fix the framework now than wait for a serious incident, such as a concealed dangerous goods case, to test it in court. By then a forwarder could be facing a claim its insurance doesn’t cover.”
In September, World Insurance told The Loadstar most forwarder liability policies already covered companies acting as both agents and principals, although forwarders should check that their cover adequately addressed the expanded liability.
AfA and the National Customs Brokers & Forwarders Association of America have published a joint white paper opposing the framework, with contributions from their Australian counterpart and support from the Canadian association. FIATA reiterated its call for a comprehensive industry review on Monday.
Mr Smith said the amendments should have awaited the review requested through FIATA.
“We expect to be part of these discussions before changes are made,” he said.
“We gave IATA notice before we published, and we’ve shared the paper with the International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations (FIATA) and with airlines directly. We’d welcome a seat at the review FIATA has asked IATA to convene.”
AfA wants the named shipper’s obligations to remain with that shipper by default, with forwarders responsible for their screening and security duties, the information they enter, their handling and customer checks.
“Airlines should keep full recourse against a forwarder that falls short on any of those. And it should be one default across carriers, not different terms on every airline,” Mr Smith said.
The white paper argues that the revised framework conflicts with the Montreal Convention. In September, HFW partner Matthew Gore told The Loadstar the provisions did not directly contradict the convention, although they could significantly expand a forwarder’s contractual exposure to the airline.
More recently, he said a UK industry association he had spoken to saw little change for most UK cargo, which generally moves under house air waybills, with forwarders already contracting directly with airlines under master air waybills.
Mr Gore had personally seen neither a claim tested under the revised provisions nor bilateral alternatives suggesting a settled market practice had emerged.
Mr Smith said AfA was not planning a legal challenge.
“Whatever the interpretation, we believe it is poor policy to put the risk on the party with the least control over the cargo, and we urge IATA to take that practical reality into account.”
AfA would continue pursuing changes with IATA and individual airlines, he added.
“If the framework doesn’t change, we’ll keep working with airlines one by one and keep our members informed on contracts and insurance.”

The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned. The meeting is now December 15.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the new date to Reuters. The Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) has already discussed Tesla’s file at two meetings without putting it to a vote.
Another date moves
Two weeks isn’t much on its own. But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.
In late 2025, Tesla told owners the Dutch regulator RDW had “committed” to approving FSD in February 2026. The RDW publicly corrected it . The Dutch approval came on April 10. Tesla then pointed owners to an EU-wide vote on October 6, and the TCMV agenda for that meeting had no vote on it .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Even the new date took a minute to settle. Belgium’s Flanders transport ministry first said the meeting had moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified it’s December 15. Nobody has given a reason for the change.
And a meeting isn’t a vote. The committee can discuss the file again and push the decision into 2027. Elon Musk said on Tesla’s Q3 call in October that he’d be surprised if EU-wide approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.
The math Tesla still needs
EU-wide approval needs at least 15 of the 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU’s population.
Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval so far: the Netherlands, Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, last week, Italy , where Tesla has started the rollout. Using Eurostat population figures, we count those 12 at roughly 29% of the EU’s population.
Germany is the obvious next yes. Berlin got Tesla to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe and then cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in exchange for its support. That would bring the yes camp to about 47%.
So Tesla still needs France, or both Spain and Poland, to get over 65%. Not a sure thing. Sweden asked the EU in June to reject the system unless Tesla removed the ability to drive above the posted limit at all.
There’s also a catch for owners. According to Reuters, an EU-level rejection would invalidate the national approvals already granted. If the vote fails, drivers in Italy, the Netherlands, and the 10 other countries who are paying for the system today could lose it.
Electrek’s Take
A two-week slip in a Brussels committee calendar isn’t too bad, but the delays are adding up. It’s December, the committee has other files, and nothing Reuters reported points to a problem specific to Tesla.
We also don’t think most owners realize what’s at stake. If this vote goes the wrong way, the national approvals go with it. Italian owners who just got the system would lose it a few weeks later.
What would help Tesla’s case more than a new name and a lower speed cap is data. The RDW still hasn’t published its test results, and Tesla has never released disengagement data in Europe or anywhere else. Governments on the fence, like Sweden, want to see evidence the system is safe, not a rebrand.
December 15 is the next date to watch. Does Tesla walk into that room with Germany, France, or Spain on board, or does this slide into 2027?

The first power purchase agreement (PPA) for space solar has been signed. Buyers, lenders, and insurers now need a way to price it.
Virtus Solis recently signed a 20-year PPA with Brae Systems to supply utility-scale solar power from orbit to data center compute infrastructure. It is the first executed PPA for space solar.
Most of the conversation about space solar still centers on technology demonstrations and capacity reservations. A signed long-term contract changes the question. For decades, engineers have asked whether power can be collected in orbit and sent to the ground. Buyers, lenders, and insurers now have to ask a more practical question: how do you underwrite it?
The answer is less exotic than it sounds. Every new-build PPA raises the same four questions. Will the technology work and get built on schedule? What happens when something fails? Who stands behind the contract? How does the power reach the meter? The PPA path to orbital solar follows the same known process with the only difference lying in the origin point of the energy.
Technology and Delivery Risk: Data Is King
Underwriting starts with what has to be proven. For orbital solar, that means three things: collecting power in orbit, transmitting it wirelessly to the ground, and converting it to grid power at a receiver. Each can be demonstrated separately, and each should be.
The right contract structure treats those demonstrations as conditions precedent. Offtake obligations switch on as the system clears defined technical gates, so the buyer never pays for power that has not been proven. The first solar, offshore wind, and early PPAs for small modular reactors were staged the same way. The industry has financed first-of-a-kind generation before, and in each case the contract made it financeable by tying commitment to evidence.
Underwriters should also ask what the underlying technology has already proven elsewhere. Space solar developers have taken different approaches to transmission, including radio-frequency and laser systems. Radio-frequency transmission, which Virtus Solis uses, relies on the same class of technology found in cell phones, where decades of component performance data already exist. Whatever the approach, the question is how much of the system’s reliability can be inferred from existing field data and how much must be shown in new demonstrations.
Delivery risk, whether the system gets built and into orbit on schedule, is driven by launch. Launch cadence has increased and launch costs have fallen sharply over the past decade, but launch availability remains the main schedule risk. Contracts should still carry the standard protections: a commercial operation date, a long-stop date, and delay damages. Modular systems can bring capacity online in tranches, with deliveries beginning on the first satellites rather than after a full constellation is in orbit. Contracts should define how partial capacity is treated during that ramp.
Lenders will focus on the gate structure and completion support. Buyers will focus on long-stop dates and their right to exit if gates are missed.
On-Orbit Failure and Insurance: An Industry That Already Exists
Space hardware fails in known ways. It can fail at launch or early in operation, it can be damaged by radiation or debris, and it degrades gradually over its life. The satellite industry has been measuring the probability of each for decades.
What changes is how those failures affect delivery. A ground plant that trips offline delivers nothing. A constellation loses capacity in increments: one failed satellite reduces output without stopping it. Forced-outage provisions should reflect that. Instead of treating an outage as a binary event, the contract should measure availability against contracted capacity and set remedies when it falls below a threshold. The replacement obligation becomes central: who pays to replace a satellite, and how quickly must capacity be restored.
The insurance market for space risk already exists. Commercial satellite operators routinely buy launch cover, first-year on-orbit cover, and in-orbit life cover. What is new is pairing that space-segment cover with the property and liability cover a power project carries on the ground. A combined product does not yet exist as a standard offering, and how it is structured will shape the cost of capital for the sector. Insurers will price the policies. Lenders will require them as a condition of financing, and buyers will care most about availability remedies.
Counterparty Considerations
A PPA is only as strong as the parties behind it, and both sides deserve scrutiny.
On the buy side, offtakers like data center operators bring load that is growing, runs around the clock, and cannot go down. Their credit varies widely, from hyperscalers to newer developers, and lenders will underwrite it accordingly. A 20-year tenor matches the life of project debt, which is the first thing a lender checks. Repeat demand matters as well. One contract proves a buyer exists, and a pipeline of contracts shows lenders the first one was not a one-off.
On the sell side, the developer is an early-stage company, as is the case with every first-of-a-kind energy project. The market has standard tools to manage that risk: credit support, step-in rights, escrow accounts, and completion guarantees. Buyers should also require performance security that covers delivery delays. Lenders will underwrite the offtaker’s credit, while buyers will underwrite the developer’s ability to deliver.
Orbital Transmission: Defining the Output Shape
This is where orbital solar looks most like a conventional power project. Power is collected in orbit and transmitted to a receiver on the ground. From the receiver, it passes through a busbar to the grid, like the output of any other plant. The receiver point sits on the ground at an asset utilities already understand.
Transmission from orbit raises two permitting questions: spectrum licensing through the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and compliance with radio-frequency exposure standards. Both are established regulatory processes with known timelines, and neither requires a new rulebook.
Receiver siting is where developers can reduce risk. Receivers placed next to data center campuses or at existing grid nodes limit exposure to new transmission lines and avoid the longest interconnection queues. Land use should be measured as energy delivered per acre rather than nameplate capacity per acre, because a receiver operates nearly around the clock.
The biggest difference from ground solar is the shape of the output. Terrestrial solar delivers on the sun’s schedule, so buyers who need firm power pay to firm it with storage, with backup generation, or with exposure to market prices after sunset. Near-continuous delivery can reduce much of that cost, along with the shape and basis risk of as-available contracts. The contract still has to define availability precisely, including any eclipse periods the orbit produces and scheduled maintenance windows.
A Proven and Familiar Framework Prices Risk
None of this requires a new discipline. Buyers, lenders, and insurers already know how to price technology risk, failure risk, counterparty risk, and delivery risk. And while the industry still needs to determine several key factors including the standard definition of availability for orbital capacity, a standard insurance product that spans orbit and ground, and a regulatory precedent for licensing spectrum for power transmission, early contracts are already beginning to set those precedents.
Data center load is growing faster than many grids can serve it, and buyers are signing long-term contracts for firm power from a widening range of sources. Orbital solar will be evaluated on the same terms as the rest: whether its risks can be identified, allocated, and priced.
— John Bucknell is founder and CEO of Virtus Solis. He was previously the SpaceX engineer responsible for the Raptor engines on Starship.

2027 Toyota Tacoma Is Mostly a Carryover, Minor Changes Cause Tiny $180 Price Bump
17 photos
Photo: Toyota
Based on when it was first released, the current generation Toyota Tacoma, the fourth, is about one-third of the way through its life cycle. This means we still have a few more years of minor nips and tucks before a major change comes along.
Exactly that's what we got this week, after the Japanese carmaker presented the 2027 model year version of the pickup truck. With these minor changes also comes a slight price bump, one that's not likely to deter customers in any way.
What Toyota focused on this time was making the package structure of the sales champion of the mid-size pickup segment, as it calls it, easier to understand and use. There are no changes to powertrain or other mechanical components.
The most noteworthy enhancements have to do with the TRD Upgrade Package and TRD Premium Package. The former now offers from the get-go the 14-inch multimedia display, while when it comes to the latter, the same screen is now offered as a standalone option, something that should lower the price of the overall package.
The revised Tacoma also throws in a power driver's seat for all four-door trims SR5 and above, and the SR5 grade is now propped on dark silver-finish alloy wheels. Last but not least, a new color called HoneyComb has been added to the TRD Pro.
Otherwise, the pickup truck continues to be the same versatile self. Built on the TNGA-F platform that's also used by the Tundra, Land Cruiser, and Sequoia, it relies on two powertrain choices to go about its business.
The first is the entry-level i-FORCE that relies on a 2.4-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine capable of delivering 278 horsepower and 317 lb.-ft. of torque.
The star of this rather limited lineup, however, is the i-FORCE MAX Hybrid, which throws in a 2.4-liter turbo engine working in conjunction with a 48-hp electric motor installed inside the eight-speed automatic transmission.
The combined output of this setup is rated at 326 horsepower and 465 lb.-ft. of torque, numbers that make it the most capable, torque-wise, ever made in the Tacoma family. This engine is, however, not meant for all the grades available.
The 2027 Toyota Tacoma will be offered in SR, SR5, TRD PreRunner, TRD Sport, TRD Off-Road, Limited, TRD Pro, and Trailhunter trims, with either a Double Cab or XtraCab cabin and a choice between a 5- or 6-foot bed.
The hybrid powertrain is only available from the get-go on the TRD Pro and Trailhunter, and optionally on the TRD Sport, TRD Off-Road, and Limited.
I said earlier the price hike is not that great. The current 2026 Tacoma sells from $32,545, while the 2027 version will retail for just $180 more, $32,725. The truck is already listed on Toyota's North American configurators.

Volkswagen gave its entry-level electric SUV a sporty makeover with GTI-inspired performance. The new ID. Cross R-Line tops the range with added power and style, but there’s more to it than meets the eye.
Volkswagen ID. Cross gets R-Line style and GTI power
The new Volkswagen ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany, starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.
While VW’s R-Line is typically just a style and equipment upgrade rather than a true performance upgrade, the range-topping ID. Cross version borrows its electric motor, battery, and chassis from the ID. Polo GTI.
The flagship ID. Cross R-Line model, which will go on sale in March 2027, will use the same 222 hp (166 kW) front-mounted electric motor with up to 290 Nm of torque, which VW said enables it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.9 seconds.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
It will also use the same 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 266 miles (428 km).
The range-topping version comes with VW’s custom chassis technology, also used in the ID. Polo GTI, which includes an electronically controlled front differential lock, DCC adaptive chassis control, and progressive steering.
As such, the flagship R-Line model is 15 mm lower than the standard ID. Cross. The lower ride height and front differential lock help to improve traction, driving stability, and control, while DCC automatically adjusts to road conditions.
The 222 hp (166 kW) version debuts with an exclusive new Traction profile with different drive modes, including Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual.
While pre-sales for the flagship version will open in March 2027, the entry-level ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.
The entry-level version uses a 132 hp (99 kW) electric motor and a 37 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 195 miles (314 km).
The entry-level version gains “extensive” R-Line standard equipment, including R-Line style bumpers, vertical daytime headlights, and 19″ alloy wheels.
Other standard features include Volkswagen’s interactive ID. Light with LED matrix headlights, Keyless Access, Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), and a rear-view camera.
Inside, all ID. Cross R-Line models feature sports comfort seats, R-Line trim, and progressive steering as standard. It also gains the Innovision Pro infotainment package with the “IDA” voice assistant.
Volkswagen has yet to reveal prices for the flagship ID. Cross R-Line with the 222 hp (166 kW) and 52 kWh battery, but it will likely be closer to €40,000 ($44,000) when it goes on sale next March. Volkswagen’s ID. Polo GTI electric hot hatch starts at €39,995.
The new R-Line trim comes after Volkswagen opened orders for the standard entry-level ID. Cross last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000).
What do you think of the new VW ID. Cross R-Line? Would you buy one in the US? Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the entry-level electric SUV to the US, but it will launch the ID. Tiguan in 2027, which will replace the ID.4 SUV.

The platform combines carrier rates, schedules, transit times, fees and surcharges to generate transportation options and pricing. Descartes said the platform pulls in the latest spot rates through application programming interfaces, or APIs, that connect directly to carriers.
Freight forwarders typically gather pricing information from carriers and compare available routes and schedules before preparing customer quotes. That process can involve searching carrier websites, collecting rates manually and working across spreadsheets. In a poll of attendees at a Descartes webinar, described in an Oct. 21 company blog post , 94% said it takes more than five minutes to prepare a quote, half said 10 to 20 minutes and 19% said more than 20. Descartes said the results reflect a selected group of freight forwarding professionals, not a formal industry survey. Digital quoting has been spreading across the industry. Freightos’ 2025 State of Online Freight report found that half of the top forwarders offered instant online quotes, compared with none in 2015.
“Speed and transparency are real competitive differentiators in freight forwarding,” said Henning Voss, vice president of product management at Descartes. “Forwarding is a fast-moving, high-pressure business. Sales teams are under significant strain, and facing huge volumes of requests from customers that require manual, time-consuming work.”
Descartes Spot consolidates those functions into one platform. Users enter an origin and destination port pairing to receive multiple transportation options with corresponding routes, departure schedules, transit times and calculated costs.
The platform also allows users to save, manage, send and track quotes. It includes configurable pricing controls and market benchmarking powered by Xeneta , a freight-rate benchmarking and market intelligence provider.
Descartes Spot is part of the company’s broader broker and forwarder enterprise systems suite, which provides technology for logistics service providers. The company said the platform is intended to let sales teams prepare quotes without relying on operations personnel to manually collect carrier rates and calculate costs.
“Leading freight forwarders are increasingly operating as growth-focused sales organizations, where responsiveness and customer experience play a larger role in winning business,” added Ken Wood, executive vice president of product management at Descartes.
Based in Waterloo, Ontario, Descartes operates the Global Logistics Network, which connects shippers, carriers and logistics service providers. Its technology portfolio includes transportation management through acquired TMS provider TAI , shipment visibility, customs compliance and supply chain data services.

Automating that work could help forwarders respond to customers faster, handle more quote requests and reduce the time employees spend on administrative tasks.

Retailers expect 19% of their holiday sales to be returned this year, and 69% anticipate more return fraud during the season, according to Happy Returns’ Returns Happen 2026 report . Shoppers surveyed expect to make 47% of their holiday purchases online, up from 43% in last year’s survey.
What’s Related
The report puts the 2026 return rate at 18% for online purchases and 9% for in-store purchases, with an overall rate of 15%. All three figures held steady from 2025. With shoppers planning to do more holiday buying online, retailers could see more merchandise return through e-commerce return channels even if return rates hold steady.
Happy Returns, a UPS company, surveyed 2,006 consumers who had returned an online purchase in the past year and 375 e-commerce professionals at U.S. retailers with at least $250 million in revenue. The report’s main retailer charts use a sample of 295 respondents.
RELATED STORIES: Holiday Inventory: How Early Is Too Early for Retailers to Buy? | Uncertain Delivery Dates Are Costing Retailers Holiday Sales, Survey Says
How to handle the holiday rush
Among retailers surveyed, 55% say they are paying closer attention to service commitments with third-party logistics providers to manage higher holiday return volumes, up from 49% in 2025 and 40% in 2024. Another 44% say they hire seasonal staff to handle returns, up from 34% two years ago.
Retailers are adjusting their policies, too. Forty-seven percent say they extend their holiday return windows, and the same share say they use stricter policies that require intact tags and receipts. Shoppers’ plans point to a concentrated rush after the holidays. Forty-five percent say they’re most likely to return an unwanted gift within two weeks to a month, and another 37% say they’ll do it within a week.
Shoppers want free returns
Free returns matter to 87% of shoppers when buying online, up from 82% in 2025. In a question about an online clothing and footwear retailer, 75% said they would be more likely to shop there if they could drop off returns nearby without a box or label. Nearly eight in 10 shoppers said they were more likely to choose a return option that starts a refund or exchange immediately.
Retailers that charge or plan to charge for returns pointed to rising processing and shipping costs. Fees average about $6 where they apply, though many retailers still offer several free ways to return a purchase. Among retailers that charge, 56% said more shoppers had switched to a free option after fees were introduced.
Fewer retailers reported a drop in return rates after adding fees. This year, 41% of retailers that charge reported a decline, down from 53% in 2025. Half reported more complaints about the fees, up from 47% last year. A poor return experience can also affect the next sale. Three-quarters of shoppers said it would make them less likely to buy from that retailer again.
Fraud complicates faster refunds
The report puts fraud at 8% of returns, unchanged from 2025. That figure covers practices such as sending back an empty box or substituting a counterfeit item. Happy Returns counts policy abuse separately, including cases where a shopper buys something, uses it and then returns it. In a separate question, 28% of shoppers said they had engaged in at least one behavior the report classified as fraud in the past year.
Improving the customer returns experience ranked first among the steps retailers say are most important to meeting their 2027 business goals, selected by 25% of respondents. Reducing fraud and losses and getting returned items back into inventory faster each drew 22%. Those goals come together at drop-off, where retailers can check what a shopper brought back before starting the refund and sending resalable items back into inventory.

NASA Needs a Nuclear Reactor for the Moon, Now Looking for Someone to Build It
9 photos
Photo: NASA
I think it's pretty obvious to anyone looking that the size and scope of NASA's plans for the Moon will need a lot more than just batteries and solar panels to sustain themselves. Luckily, there is one more solution the agency can turn to: nuclear reactors.
Having already proven their merits here on Earth, nuclear reactors might just as well do the same on the lunar surface, acting as a source of electricity. If only there were someone able and willing to build one...
In the bid to find an answer to that question, the American space agency announced earlier this week that it is looking for industry partners to work on such a design. We don't have all the details of what is actually required, but the little bits of info that have been presented already are quite interesting.
Without going full-reveal on specifics, NASA said it requires a small fission power system capable of generating 20 kilowatts of electricity. On the Moon, that should be enough to feed power to future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and whatever other infrastructure will be built up there.
For reference, 20 kilowatts of power is enough here on Earth to keep 16 average households afloat for an entire year. A mighty reactor, then, which could prove invaluable for the needs of building the Moon base.
The agency calls the design the Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), and intends to launch it to the Moon as soon as possible. Once delivered to the lunar surface, it should be able to operate without human intervention for as much as five years.
And it could do that even during the lunar night, which lasts for two weeks on the Moon, seeing how it doesn't need solar power to do its thing. NASA is accepting proposals on the reactor by December 21, and says it could issue additional task orders for other nuclear power systems that it might require to fulfill its needs.
In fact, if you really think about it, NASA has already done so when it announced the Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom in late October. The name was slapped on both a spacecraft meant to deliver a trio of exploration helicopters collectively called SkyFall to Mars, and the reactor that powers it.
NASA didn't provide us with all the details of the SR-1, but we're dealing with a system that generates heat through nuclear fission and, thanks to a conversion system, turns that heat into electricity that's then fed to the ship's power systems and electric propulsion.
When it gets going, the Freedom will become the first fission-powered spacecraft to venture beyond Earth's orbit. The mission, which is expected to get going sometime in 2028, will also be used to inform the design of the Lunar Reactor-1.

Previously rumored to feature a reworked 2.9-liter V6 from the RS 4/RS 5, which Audi might have tested at some point, the RS 6 is actually packing the 4.0-liter V8 we all know and love. That's not all, though.
On the right-side rear quarter panel, we can see the fuel filler door. Opposite, the German automaker integrated the charging port on the driver-side rear quarter panel. Because it's related to the RS 5 under the skin, prospective customers may be presented with 25.9 kWh gross at the very least.

More specifically, the RS 5 uses a hybridized ZF eight-speed automatic. The P2 layout should carry over to the RS 6, with P2 meaning electric motor housed between the transmission and engine, inside the bell housing. A separating clutch disconnects the internal combustion engine so the vehicle can be driven on pure electric power without any kind of engine drag.
Photo: Baldauf These latest spy photos of the 2028 model year RS 6 also reveal that Audi has decided on a four-door body rather than five doors for the RS 5 sedan. Indeed, the RS 5 is a liftback by default. It's been 16 years since the C6-generation RS 6 sedan left us, with remaining stock lasting until 2011.

The RS 6 should also borrow quattro with Dynamic Torque Control from the RS 5, specifically an all-wheel-drive system with an electromechanical torque-vectoring rear differential. Instead of hydraulic clutches, a water-cooled electric actuator that runs at 400 volts does the heavy lifting.
Because it operates independently of the engine, said permanent-magnet actuator can shift a lot of torque to the outside rear wheel to help the car turn sharper. Wider than the S6, the RS 6 retains the full-width LED taillight setup of lesser A6 family members.
The standard light bar features choreographed unlocking and locking animations, while the available OLED lights double as an external display. All segments automatically illuminate at full brightness when another vehicle approaches within two meters of a stationary A6 optioned with these lights.
Visually distinct from the poor-selling RS e-tron GT and the S6 e-tron , the RS 6 will reach US dealers in both sedan and Avant body styles. source_document.body:
The federal crash file has spent most of 2026 telling the trucking industry a comforting story, one in which the number of serious commercial vehicle crashes keeps sliding from its 2022 peak, the safety spending fleets made during the freight recession appears to be paying off, and the holiday stretch ahead reads like a few more weeks of the same quiet decline. SONAR counts 178,512 federal recordable crashes in 2025, down 10.5% from 199,395 in 2022 . Over roughly the same three years, the number of carriers holding operating authority fell 11.4%. Fewer crashes isn’t the same thing necessarily as safer trucking.
SONAR counts 140,247 federal recordable crashes involving trucks and buses so far in 2026, and 3,411 of them were fatal. November’s steep drop comes from states uploading crash reports late, not from safer roads, since they have up to 90 days to report. (Chart: FreightWaves SONAR Carrier Safety, data through Nov. 24, 2026)
A crash is federal recordable when it involves a commercial motor vehicle and ends in a death , an injury serious enough that someone is transported from the scene for treatment, or a vehicle towed away with disabling damage. That threshold screens out the parking-lot scrapes and mirror strikes, so every crash in this file is an event that cost somebody a truck, a hospital trip or a life. In 2025, 2.58% of those crashes were fatal and 37.55% involved an injury. Those full-year shares are the baseline for judging the holidays.
Start with what the optimists have right, then put a denominator under it. From December 2022 to December 2025, the count of property carriers with operating authority fell 11.4%, according to FTR’s analysis of FMCSA data and Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll employment in truck transportation fell 4.7%. The crash counts run by calendar year while those capacity measures run December to December, so the periods differ slightly . Per carrier, total crashes were flat. Per payroll worker, they fell about 6%.
Fatal crashes are a different story, and the industry has earned credit for it. SONAR counts 4,603 fatal crashes in 2025, down 25% from 6,133 in 2022, more than twice the pace at which carriers left. That works out to roughly 15% fewer fatal crashes per carrier and 21% fewer per payroll worker. One caution: the state-reported federal file counts more fatal crashes than NHTSA’s fatality census, which FMCSA puts at 5,252 involving large trucks in 2022 , plus 197 involving buses. The size of the drop deserves a second check. Its direction is hard to argue with.
Truck miles would be the better denominator, and the federal government publishes them with a long lag. The most recent per-mile figures, the National Safety Council’s analysis of 2024 NHTSA data , put large trucks in injury crashes at 37 per 100 million large-truck miles, up 5.7% from 2023. The fatal involvement rate fell 3% from 2023 but sits 9% above its level a decade earlier. That is a mixed record, not a safety story.
The 2026 numbers can’t be set against those full years yet, and not only because the year isn’t over. FMCSA requires states to upload crash reports to its Motor Carrier Management Information System within 90 days, and its State Safety Data Quality ratings now grade states on the share that arrive within 45. SONAR’s monthly trend shows November 2026 at a small fraction of October’s count, and October is likely still filling in. Those aren’t safer weeks. They’re uncounted ones.
Capacity is still leaving, too. SONAR’s count of tractors in for-hire fleets stood at 1,551,161 as of Nov. 13, down about 107,000 from a year earlier , and about 51,000 of them left in August 2026 alone . Some of 2026’s lower crash count is simply fewer trucks on the road. That makes this year’s raw counts close to useless for year-over-year comparison.
The honest holiday comparison holds the fleet roughly constant by staying inside one year, and the for-hire carrier population was largely unchanged across 2025 , according to FMCSA data. SONAR shows 16,386 federal recordable crashes in December 2025, 10% above 2025’s monthly average of 14,876, and 414 fatal crashes, 8% above the monthly average of 384. November went the other way, at 13,910 crashes, 6.5% below average. The holiday problem is December.
December’s crashes weren’t deadlier, just more numerous. Its fatal share was 2.53%, slightly below 2025’s full-year 2.58%, while November’s was 2.65%, and neither gap is large enough to build on. Shares aren’t immune to reporting lag either. If fatal crash reports reach the federal file faster or slower than tow-away reports, a partial year’s share is skewed, which is why 2026’s year-to-date fatal share of 2.43% isn’t a fair comparison yet. December’s risk is volume, and volume is something carriers can plan around.
Van, reefer and enclosed trailers account for 65,782 of the year’s federal recordable crashes, about 47%. Body type went unreported in 19,066 crashes. Hazmat releases drop off sharply in November because states haven’t uploaded those reports yet. (Chart: FreightWaves SONAR Carrier Safety, data through Nov. 24, 2026)
The holiday freight runs where the crashes already are
SONAR’s cargo body breakdown for 2026 puts 65,782 crashes, 46.9% of the year’s total, on van, reefer and enclosed equipment. In 19,066 crashes, 13.6% of the file, the body type simply wasn’t reported, which is its own quiet indictment of crash report quality. To be clear, the van share mostly reflects the size of the van fleet, and this data doesn’t show that vans crash more per mile than flatbeds. What it does show is where the exposure lives. The holiday surge in retail and grocery freight adds miles to exactly that segment.
Geography concentrates the raw count. Texas logged more than twice as many federal recordable crashes as any other state in SONAR’s 2026 data. Raw counts aren’t rates, though. Texas has more road miles, more trucks and more freight than any other state, and without state-level truck miles there’s no fair way to call it more dangerous.
Why it matters
The strongest objection is that a crash file isn’t a safety verdict. A federal recordable crash is not a fault determination, and FMCSA’s Crash Preventability Determination Program exists because counting every crash against every carrier overstates the carrier’s role. All of that is true. None of it changes the math. More trucks running more miles produce more serious crashes no matter who caused them, and carriers absorb the insurance, downtime and safety-score consequences either way.
Here is what would prove us wrong. Once December 2026 is fully reported, which under the 90-day requirement means by late March 2027, its premium over 2026’s own monthly average should come in well under last year’s 10%. If it does, the seasonal spike has flattened. A lower raw count, by itself, proves only that there are fewer trucks. We will rerun the numbers in the spring.
Until then, carriers should plan December around last year’s 10% premium rather than this year’s trend line. That means building slack into van and reefer retail runs instead of dispatching drivers to the edge of their hours of service through the holiday stretch. Brokers covering holiday surge freight should check a carrier’s crash history on every lane before tendering, not after a claim. Shippers holding rigid appointment windows through the holidays should understand that detention and missed slots push drivers to make up time on the road, and that cost lands on someone else’s highway.
FMCSA owes the industry something too. The agency should publish crash counts beside an exposure measure, active power units or truck miles, along with each state’s reporting timeliness, instead of leaving timeliness inside the State Safety Data Quality ratings. A count without a denominator invites exactly the misreading this year’s file is producing. A quiet November in the crash file is paperwork in transit. December will be counted.

Freight fraud trends and what they cost shippers
How hijacked carrier identities, a tight truckload market and a shifting liability landscape put shippers on the front line of cargo theft.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Freight fraud no longer depends on fake carriers. In Q3 2026, more than 80% of the stolen loads reported to Highway involved real carrier credentials in the wrong hands: hijacked inboxes, purchased motor carrier authorities and rogue carriers with clean records. Reported theft counts fell from Q2 at both Highway and Verisk CargoNet, but the value of each theft is climbing, and the operational burden is moving down the chain to the shipper’s dock. National truckload tender rejections (STRI.USA) sit at 12.78%, roughly double the 6.3% of a year ago; reefer rejections ( STRIR.USA ) are near 22%; and Q4 has historically added another leg higher. Robinson verdict (now above $700M with interest) raises broker risk costs that are likely to flow into shipper rates and routing guides.

Insights from Supply Chain Day at F3 2026, plus the SONAR data behind them
Published: November 2026 | GoSONAR.com | Data Source: SONAR
Volatility is a finance problem now
Supply chain volatility used to show up on the loading dock. In 2026, it shows up in the budget variance report. That was the starting point for the fireside chat that kicked off Supply Chain Day at F3 2026 in Chattanooga on Monday, Oct. 26. Two speakers who think in spreadsheets as much as in lanes took the stage:
Craig Decker , Head of Transportation & Logistics Services and Infrastructure at Brown Gibbons Lang & Company (BGL). He has spent decades advising on M&A and capital markets deals across trucking, rail, maritime and logistics.
Zach Strickland , Director of Freight Market Intelligence at SONAR. He holds a finance degree and started his career in banking before moving into truckload and LTL pricing and analytics.
Over about 23 minutes, they covered three threads: where the freight market stands today, how M&A across freight and freight technology is reshaping the industry, and how finance leaders can stay steady with better data and longer planning horizons.
A month later, with Thanksgiving freight moving and 2027 bids on the table, their framing matters more than it did on stage. Here’s why.
The data: rejections doubled and stayed there
Carriers are turning down about twice as many contracted loads as they did a year ago, and that rate has not come back down. SONAR data shows the shift:
Measure | Nov 2025 avg | Nov 2026 avg (thru Nov 24) | Change
Tender rejections ( STRI.USA ) | 6.8% | 13.0% | +6.2 pts
Tender volume ( STVI.USA ) | 10,196 | 11,286 | +11%
The peak came in June. STRI averaged 17.0% for the month and topped out near 17.7%.
The plateau is the story. STRI has averaged between 13% and 14% every month from August through November.
In budget terms: about 1 in 8 contracted loads is being rejected and pushed to a backup carrier or the spot market . That is a cost the original contract rate never priced in.
Decker put the moment in perspective:
“I haven’t seen our transport costs rise this much on a material basis in the 30 years I’ve been doing this.” CRAIG DECKER, BROWN GIBBONS LANG & COMPANY
His view is that shippers should plan for a high-cost environment that lasts a while, not a spike that fades by spring.
Source: SONAR, STRI.USA and STVI.USA monthly averages, pulled Nov 25, 2026.
The dealmaker’s view: capital follows defensible freight
This market is tightening because capacity is leaving, not because demand is booming. That changes who survives and who buys whom.
Buyers are paying up, but selectively. Median transportation and logistics deal multiples rose from 9.5x to 10.2x EBITDA in early 2026, per PwC data reported by CCJ .
Decker’s take on truckload: deal interest centers on high-margin, recurring shipper revenue. That means dedicated contract carriage and resilient end markets like healthcare, pharma and cold chain ( CCJ ).
Decker’s take on LTL: density wins. Larger carriers will pick up smaller, less-capitalized networks, and rising operating costs push more small carriers to sell.
Broker risk is rising too. The Supreme Court’s Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II ruling lets negligent-selection claims against brokers proceed. Documented carrier vetting is now a balance-sheet issue.
On stage, the conversation widened beyond carriers and brokers to freight technology. Financial pressure and strategic interest are driving consolidation there too, reshaping who owns the data and tools shippers rely on.
What this means for shippers: the carrier or broker in your routing guide today may be acquired, merged or gone by the time your 2027 contract ends.
Before 2027 bids lock: six questions for the CFO
A freight budget should be built around the routing guide you will actually get, not the contract rates on paper.
What does a failed tender cost us? Model your budget with 13% of loads falling to backup carriers or spot, not 0%.
How much spot exposure can we carry? Decide on a target share before the RFP, then price contracts against it.
Are our carriers financially durable? Check fleet trends, ownership and safety records on key lanes, not just rate.
Can our brokers show their vetting? After Montgomery, ask for documented carrier diligence on your freight.
Where can we change mode or contract type? Shift eligible lanes to intermodal or from spot to contract where the data supports it.
When did we last read our MSAs and payment terms? Old agreements, default pay cycles and unchecked surcharges often leave money on the table.
The overlooked levers: payables and line items
Decker’s most concrete advice had nothing to do with rates. He urged shippers to review the full chain, from the business development team that sets contract terms to the clerk who pays invoices and sends the checks.
Reopen old MSAs. Decker cited a $3 million savings found by reviewing legacy master service agreements and putting the balance sheet, both your own and a partner’s, to better use.
Use the pay cycle. Short-pay terms can be a real source of value. As Decker put it: “Are we taking advantage of all of the discounts available for short pay?”
Audit every line item. Know exactly what you pay for, and watch fuel surcharges closely. Decker described savings from renegotiating fuel surcharges to regional PADD diesel prices, so the charge tracked actual fuel costs more closely.
Why now: With interest rates this high, an early-pay discount can return more than cash sitting idle, and carriers value fast payment more than ever.
That was the through-line of the fireside chat: stability comes from better data and longer planning horizons, not from guessing the next swing. Market intelligence platforms like SONAR let teams act before volatility shows up in the numbers, not after.
The bottom line
The operational shocks of 2026 have mostly settled into a financial pattern: higher rejections, rising costs and a carrier base that keeps consolidating. The shippers who do well in 2027 will be the ones whose finance and transportation teams read the same data before the bids close.

Artist's impression of the new terminal (Photo: APM Terminals)
By Gavin van Marle
25 November 2026
APM Terminals and the port of Rotterdam have unveiled plans to add a further 1.4m teu of capacity to the operator’s flagship Maasvlakte II facility in the Dutch hub.
With the terminal’s first phase of expansion recently completed, the new second phase will see a further 711 metres of quay built and 25ha of terminal yard space added.
“This expansion marks the next step in the long-term development of our terminal,” said Harold Kunst, managing director, APM Terminals, Maasvlakte II.
“We are creating space for future growth while continuing to develop a terminal that can serve our customers safely, reliably, and efficiently over the long term.
“Our collaboration with the Port of Rotterdam Authority is essential to achieving this. Together, we are laying the foundations for the next phase of Maasvlakte II,” he added.
However, formal approval for the terminal and the necessary investment by the port authority still requires its shareholders – comprising Rotterdam municipality with 70% and the national government with the remaining 30% – to vote for it unanimously, which is currently expected to be granted in February 2027.
As per usual in the landlord port model, the port authority will be responsible for funding and constructing the quay walls as well as dredging the access channel – the project is expected to require some 1.3m cu metres of sand to be dredged.
“The further development of APM Terminals Maasvlakte II marks an important step in our shared ambition to prepare the Port of Rotterdam for the future,” Boudewijn Siemons, chief executive of the Port of Rotterdam Authority, said.
“By investing in additional capacity and modern infrastructure, we are strengthening Rotterdam’s position as Europe’s leading container port.
“In doing so, we are increasing the resilience of logistics chains, contributing to security of supply for businesses and consumers, and strengthening the competitiveness of the Dutch economy,” he added.
Assuming it wins port authority shareholder approval, construction of the new area will begin in October 2027 and is scheduled to be completed by January 2030.
While the current APMT Maasvlakte II terminal is one of the key nodes in Gemini’s hub-and-spoke network, it has been constrained by its capacity so far – it hosts four of the partnership’s Asia-North Europe loops, but has only recently, with the opening of the phase one expansion, begun to service other Gemini trades.
In October the first of Gemini’s four North Europe-North America transatlantic services, the AL1, moved from the nearby Hutchison Delta facility to APMT, and the second phase of expansion will clearly allow the Gemini partners to consolidate more of their calls there.
The development will likely take Rotterdam’s overall capacity near 25m teu per year. According to Xeneta’s eeSea platform, other terminal improvements in Rotterdam will take combined capacity up to 23.3m teu a year by 2030, before the additional AMPT capacity is factored in.
Meanwhile, in the first nine months of this year total container throughput at Rotterdam hit 10.7m teu, which was just 0.1% up on the same period in 2025 – with an 8.9% increase in laden imports and a 1% growth in laden exports offset by a 20% decline in transhipment boxes.
“Due to long-standing capacity restraints at deep-sea terminals in Rotterdam, more cargo is being handled via other ports,” the port authority noted.

Visiting months after a recall of tablets made at the Indian plant, FDA inspectors identified problems with Alkem’s investigations of unexpected dissolution test results, among other issues.
The FDA has sent Alkem Laboratories a warning letter after inspectors found fault with its investigations of quality signals, responses to complaints and equipment maintenance.
FDA inspectors assessed Alkem’s plant in western India in April and May, according to the letter dated Nov. 18. The inspection began months after Ascend Laboratories recalled batches of atorvastatin, the statin medicine sold by Pfizer as Lipitor and manufactured for the U.S. market by Alkem. Ascend recalled more than 141,000 bottles because the tablets failed dissolution specifications.
The FDA inspection revealed that Alkem failed to adequately investigate unexpected discrepancies. A 2021 feasibility study linked excipients from new suppliers to a notable decrease in the dissolution rate of certain tablets, the name of which is redacted in the warning letter. Alkem saw a markedly lower dissolution rate for a tablet batch manufactured in July 2022 with excipients from the new suppliers.
But the company only investigated the quality signal after obtaining out-of-specification dissolution results during release testing of batches in March 2025, the FDA found. The investigation identified batch-to-batch inconsistency of excipients from new suppliers as the probable cause. Alkem recalled tablets manufactured from July 2024 to August 2025 for the U.S. market.
The FDA concluded that Alkem’s manufacturing process for the tablets is not in a state of control. That conclusion reflects the failures of multiple batches to meet dissolution specifications since 2021. The FDA identified a pattern of establishing or changing process parameters without adequate scientific justification, leading the agency to suggest that Alkem has a deficient process validation program.
Manufacturing
